title: Scalar Variables - Numbers & Evaluate
description: MENTOR-9: "Text variables are useful, but robots need to do math. Power calculations, distance measurements, resource counts—all require numeric variables and the Evaluate keyword."

story.setup: The ship's power systems need calibration. MENTOR-9 pulls up a diagnostic readout.
story.context: "PROTO-7, we need to calculate total power output. We have three reactors, each producing different amounts. We can't just log numbers—we need to DO MATH on them. That's where the Evaluate keyword comes in."
story.success: MENTOR-9: "Excellent! You've performed calculations with Evaluate. Addition, subtraction, multiplication, division—all the basic operations. This is how robots think numerically!"

instructions: Create a test case named 'Power Calculations'
Create a variable '${reactor_1}' with value 150 (use Set Variable)
Use Evaluate to calculate total power: '${reactor_1} + ${reactor_2} + ${reactor_3}' and store in '${total_power}'
Use Evaluate to calculate average power: '${total_power} / 3' and store in '${average_power}'
Use Evaluate to calculate power deficit: '600 - ${total_power}' and store in '${deficit}'
Log the total power with message: 'Total power: 525'
Log the average power with message: 'Average power: 175.0'
Log the deficit with message: 'Power deficit: 75'
Run the code and inspect the Console tab to see calculated values
hints: You can use variables in expressions: ${var1} + ${var2}

theory.title: Scalar Variables: Numbers & Math with Evaluate
theory.content:
MENTOR-9 gestures to the ship's power distribution panel, numbers flickering across holographic displays.

MENTOR-9: "Look at this. Three reactors, different outputs. We can't manually calculate the total every time. We need the computer to do the math. That's what Evaluate does—it performs calculations."

Numeric Variables

Variables can store numbers just like they store text:

${count}    Set Variable    42
${temperature}    Set Variable    -15
${distance}    Set Variable    3.14159

But storing numbers isn't enough—we need to calculate with them.

The Evaluate Keyword

Evaluate executes Python expressions and returns the result. It's Robot Framework's calculator.

${result}    Evaluate    10 + 5
Log    ${result}    # Outputs: 15

Math Operations

  • Addition: Evaluate 10 + 5 → 15
  • Subtraction: Evaluate 10 - 5 → 5
  • Multiplication: Evaluate 10 * 5 → 50
  • Division: Evaluate 10 / 5 → 2.0
  • Integer Division: Evaluate 10 // 3 → 3
  • Modulo (remainder): Evaluate 10 % 3 → 1
  • Exponentiation: Evaluate 2 ** 3 → 8

Using Variables in Calculations

The real power comes from using variables in expressions:

${width}    Set Variable    10
${height}    Set Variable    5
${area}    Evaluate    ${width} * ${height}
Log    Area: ${area}    # Outputs: Area: 50

Robot Framework replaces ${width} and ${height} with their values before evaluating.

Complex Expressions

You can combine multiple operations:

${total}    Evaluate    (${a} + ${b}) * ${c} / 2
${average}    Evaluate    (${x} + ${y} + ${z}) / 3
${percentage}    Evaluate    (${part} / ${whole}) * 100

Standard mathematical operator precedence applies (multiplication/division before addition/subtraction).

Why Evaluate Instead of Built-in Math Keywords?

Robot Framework doesn't have built-in keywords like "Add" or "Multiply." Instead, it uses Evaluate to leverage Python's powerful expression evaluation.

Advantages:

  • No need to learn separate math keywords
  • Use familiar mathematical notation
  • Access to full Python math capabilities
  • Can evaluate complex expressions in one line

Common Use Cases

# Calculate total cost
${total_cost}    Evaluate    ${quantity} * ${price}

# Convert Celsius to Fahrenheit
${fahrenheit}    Evaluate    (${celsius} * 9/5) + 32

# Calculate percentage
${pass_rate}    Evaluate    (${passed} / ${total}) * 100

# Increment a counter
${counter}    Evaluate    ${counter} + 1

Important Notes

  • Evaluate returns float for division: 10 / 3 = 3.333...
  • Use // for integer division: 10 // 3 = 3
  • Variables must already exist before using in Evaluate
  • Python syntax rules apply inside Evaluate
